title: The sages' mountain
hookLine: Isigili, the mountain that swallowed the sages, and the names of the silent Buddhas
carry: a mountain that seemed to swallow them

lines: ONE HILL NEVER CHANGED ITS NAME.
cards: Rajgir, in the Indian state of Bihar, sits in a ring of low, rocky hills. In the Buddha's day it was Rajagaha, a royal city, and pilgrims still climb those hills today.

In the hundred and sixteenth discourse, the Buddha is staying on one of them, called Isigili. He points out the hills around them to the monks, one by one, and says each had another name long ago. All but one.
Isigili, he says, has always been called Isigili. And then he tells them why.

teach.b: Isigili means something like the sage-swallower: isi is a seer or sage, gili is swallowing.
Long ago, the Buddha says, five hundred silent Buddhas lived on this mountain. People saw them go up into it, and never saw them come out. So they said: this mountain swallows the sages.

The name stuck. A silent Buddha, a paccekabuddha, is a figure in Buddhist tradition who wakes up on their own, in an age with no Buddha teaching, and doesn't found a community or spread a teaching the way the Buddha did.
Then the discourse becomes a roll call. The Buddha recites their names. Arittha.
Sudassana. On and on, with short phrases of praise: the free one, the one without craving, the one who ended birth. No stories about them, none of their teachings.
Just names, spoken on a hill. Why keep such a list? One way to hear it: awakening isn't owned by the well-known.
There were whole generations of free people whose only record is a name, and a mountain that seemed to swallow them.
The Buddha takes the time to say each name aloud, the way a family still says the name of a grandparent who never gave a speech. The hills are still there, and so are the names.

how: Pilgrims to Rajgir in Bihar visit the hills around the old city of Rajagaha, including Vulture's Peak, and in Theravada tradition the paccekabuddhas are honored as fully awakened beings who appear when no Buddha's teaching is known.

games.q: people see five hundred sages climb into the mountain and never come out. what do they call it?
games.why: Isigili: the mountain that swallows the sages. Vulture's Peak is a different hill nearby.

practice: Let your eyes rest on a hill, a tall building or a line of trees, or picture one, and let the breath be slow. Think how long that shape has stood, and how many quiet lives have passed beside it without anyone writing them down.
If you like, say silently the name of one quiet person you've known.

wordCard.voice: Isigili. The mountain near Rajagaha named for silent Buddhas who went into it and never came out, remembered in the discourse by their names.

orig.note: Pali Isigili: from isi, sage, and gili, swallowing. a hill near Rajagaha.

carryVoice: Your line: a mountain that seemed to swallow them. Quiet goodness is remembered too. That's day four eighty-six.
